::: {.in-short}
**In short.** We asked `r n_q` questions about Finnish history and searched the national
heritage portal Finna for each one in three ways: with our own words only, with extra words
suggested by a computer, and with official thesaurus terms in Finnish, Swedish and English.
**How we searched changed what we found.** For the middle question, the fullest search (C)
matched **`r times(med_C)`** as many records as our own words did, and
the records it showed were **mostly different ones**. It brought forward Finnish- and
Swedish-language material and other museums and archives. People still need to check whether
those records are *better*, and whether the AI's answers are right.
:::

## What is this study about?

Historians and other researchers now find most of their sources through computer systems.
Between a research question and the evidence on the screen there are several hidden steps:
catalogues from many institutions, lists of official subject words, automatic indexing
tools and, more and more, AI that writes summaries.

These steps help, but they also make choices for us. They decide which words count, which
records come first and which collections appear at all. This study makes those steps
**visible** and measures **what each step changes**.

## The three ways of searching

Think of asking a library for material on *how women were shown in Finnish advertising,
1920 to 1960*. We picked two key words, **women** and **advertising**, and searched in three
ways:

<span class="cond cond-a">Search A: your own words using Finna</span>
We search for exactly the words we chose.

::: {.query style="--c:#3A5A78"}
`r q_of("A_direct")`
:::

<span class="cond cond-b">Search B: your words + the indexer's suggestions</span>
A computer tool called **Annif** reads the question and suggests subject words, the way a
cataloguer would. We add the suggestions that fit one of our words.

::: {.query style="--c:#2E8B7A"}
`r q_of("B_annif")`
:::

<span class="cond cond-c">Search C: B + official thesaurus terms</span>
The national thesaurus **YSO** (looked up through the **Finto** service) gives the official
name of each idea in Finnish, Swedish and English. We add those as well.

::: {.query style="--c:#8A5A9E"}
`r q_of("C_finto")`
:::

`AND` means "both must appear" and `OR` means "any of these will do". So every search keeps
the whole topic (women *and* advertising); the searches differ only in **how many ways of
saying each idea** they accept.

## What we did

1. We wrote `r n_q` research questions on different topics and periods, each with two key words.
2. We searched Finna in the three ways above, with the same year range for all three.
3. From each search we kept the **top 60 records**, in Finna's own order.
4. We recorded *why* each record was found: which word matched it.
5. An AI model (OpenAI) read the **top 8 records** of each search and wrote a short answer,
   citing the records it used.
6. We compared the three searches, and the three answers, with each other.
